```{r echo = T, results = 'hide'}
Sys.setenv("DISPLAY"=":0")
library(dplyr)
library(Seurat)
library(data.table)
```
```{r}
# Load the DC Day 3 RNA dataset
d3.data <- Read10X(data.dir = "../rna_d3/outs/filtered_feature_bc_matrix/")
# 8734 cells
# Initialize the Seurat object with the raw (non-normalized) data.
d3 <- CreateSeuratObject(counts = d3.data, project = "DC", min.cells = 3, min.features = 200)
# 8696 cells
```

```{r}
# The [[ operator can add columns to object metadata. This is a great place to stash QC stats
# check the percentage of mitochondria genes
d3[["percent.mt"]] <- PercentageFeatureSet(d3, pattern = "^mt-")
```

```{r}
# preview a few cells and genes
d3.data[c("mt-Nd1", "mt-Nd2", "mt-Co1"), 1:30]
# Show QC metrics for the first 5 cells, mito genes, etc.
head(d3@meta.data, 5)
tail(d3@meta.data[order(d3@meta.data$percent.mt),],10)
mtHighExample <- d3.data[,'TCGGGCATCGCATAGT']
mtHighExample[mtHighExample != 0]
```

```{r}
# Visualize QC metrics as a violin plot
VlnPlot(d3, features = c("nFeature_RNA", "nCount_RNA", "percent.mt"), ncol = 3, pt.size = 0, log = TRUE)
```
```{r}
# FeatureScatter is typically used to visualize feature-feature relationships, but can be used
# for anything calculated by the object, i.e. columns in object metadata, PC scores etc.

plot1 <- FeatureScatter(d3, feature1 = "nFeature_RNA", feature2 = "percent.mt", pt.size = 0.1)
plot2 <- FeatureScatter(d3, feature1 = "nFeature_RNA", feature2 = "nCount_RNA", pt.size = 0.1)
CombinePlots(plots = list(plot1, plot2))
```

```{r}

plot2 <- FeatureScatter(d3, feature1 = "nFeature_RNA", feature2 = "nCount_RNA", pt.size = 0.1)
```

```{r}
data_to_write_out <- as.data.frame(as.matrix(d3@assays$RNA@counts))
```

```{r}
## read output from python/scrublet and add scrublet score and call to d3
scrub <- read.table("scrublet_d3.csv", sep=",", header=TRUE)
d3 <- AddMetaData(
  object = d3,
  metadata = scrub$doublet_score,
  col.name = 'scrubScore'
)
d3 <- AddMetaData(
  object = d3,
  metadata = scrub$predicted_doublet,
  col.name = 'scrubCall'
)
plot1 <- FeatureScatter(d3, feature1 = "nFeature_RNA", feature2 = "percent.mt", pt.size = 0.1)
plot2 <- FeatureScatter(d3, feature1 = "scrubScore", feature2 = "percent.mt", pt.size = 0.1)
CombinePlots(plots = list(plot1, plot2))
```

## De-multiplex

Seurat automatic algorithm did not work very well. My cells have double positive and hash2 bleeds into hash1.

```{r}
# read output from CITE-seq-count python package counted antibody barcode data. Required from Totalseq-A antibodies. For Totalseq-B and -C, they are included in cell ranger counted data.
d3Hto <- Read10X(data.dir = "../citeseq/d3HtoCount/umi_count/", gene.column = 1)
#Save only 2 meaningful hashtags for day 3.
d3Hto <- d3Hto[1:2,]
d3Hto <- d3Hto[,d3Hto[1,]<3000] # filter out large count cells
rownames(d3Hto) <- substring(rownames(d3Hto), 1, 5) #truncate row names
# Select cell barcodes detected by both RNA and HTO In the example datasets we have already
joint.bcs <- intersect(colnames(d3), colnames(d3Hto))
# Subset RNA and HTO counts by joint cell barcodes
d3 <- d3[, joint.bcs]  #7626 cells
d3Hto <- d3Hto[, joint.bcs]

# Confirm that the HTO have the correct names
rownames(d3Hto)

# Add HTO data as a new assay independent from RNA
d3[["HTO"]] <- CreateAssayObject(counts = d3Hto)
# Normalize HTO data, here we use centered log-ratio (CLR) transformation
d3 <- NormalizeData(d3, assay = "HTO", normalization.method = "CLR")

FeatureScatter(d3, feature1 = "Hash1", feature2 = "Hash2")
```
```{r}
### manual Demux


# testing: Hash not a straight line, do compensation subtract 5% Hash2 from Hash1, add 0.3 to stay > 0.
d3temp <- d3
d3temp@assays$HTO@data[1,] <- d3temp@assays$HTO@data[1,] - 0.05 * d3temp@assays$HTO@data[2,]+0.3
FeatureScatter(d3temp, feature1 = "Hash1", feature2= "Hash2")
d3temp1 <- subset(d3temp, hto_Hash2 >= 0.6)
hist(d3temp1@assays$HTO@data[1,],breaks =50) #Hash1 >0.9 test to find best cutoff
d3temp2 <- subset(d3temp, hto_Hash1 >= 0.9)
hist(d3temp2@assays$HTO@data[2,],breaks =50) #Hash2 >0.6 test to find best cutoff
d3temp <- subset(d3temp, ( hto_Hash1>0.9) & (hto_Hash2>0.6), invert = TRUE) # remove double positive
d3temp <- subset(d3temp, ( hto_Hash1<0.6) & (hto_Hash2<0.4), invert = TRUE) # remove double negative
d3temp@assays$HTO@data[1,] <- d3temp@assays$HTO@data[1,] + 0.05 * d3temp@assays$HTO@data[2,] - 0.3 # de-compensation

d3temp <- HTODemux(d3temp, assay = "HTO", positive.quantile = 0.99, init = 2) # do auto-deMux

d3 <- d3temp # 7361 cells
# Global classification results
table(d3$HTO_classification.global)
# Group cells based on the max HTO signal and plot
Idents(d3) <- "HTO_maxID"
RidgePlot(d3, assay = "HTO", features = rownames(d3[["HTO"]])[1:2], ncol = 1)
FeatureScatter(d3, feature1 = "Hash1", feature2 = "Hash2")
```

## Analyse Day 3 data
```{r}
d3 <- NormalizeData(d3)
# Select the top 1000 most variable features
d3 <- FindVariableFeatures(d3, selection.method = "mean.var.plot")

# Scaling RNA data, we only scale the variable features here for efficiency
d3 <- ScaleData(d3, features = VariableFeatures(d3))

# Run PCA
d3 <- RunPCA(d3, features = VariableFeatures(d3))

## Store in d3temp here
# d3temp <- d3 #968.5Mb

#View PCA
VizDimLoadings(d3, dims = 1:4, reduction = "pca")

## In particular DimHeatmap allows for easy exploration of the primary sources of heterogeneity in a dataset, and can be useful when trying to decide which PCs to include for further downstream analyses. Both cells and features are ordered according to their PCA scores. Setting cells to a number plots the ‘extreme’ cells on both ends of the spectrum, which dramatically speeds plotting for large datasets. Though clearly a supervised analysis, we find this to be a valuable tool for exploring correlated feature sets.

DimHeatmap(d3, dims = 1:15, cells = 500, balanced = TRUE)
```

```{r}
## Determine the ‘dimensionality’ of the dataset
# JackStraw procedure
d3 <- JackStraw(d3, num.replicate = 100, dims = 50)
d3 <- ScoreJackStraw(d3, dims = 1:40)

# 'Significant' PCs will show a strong enrichment of features with low p-values (solid curve above the dashed line). 
JackStrawPlot(d3, dims = 1:40)

```
```{r}
ElbowPlot(d3, ndims = 40)
```

```{r}
# to restore d3
#d3 <- d3temp  
# We select the top 10 PCs for clustering and tSNE based on PCElbowPlot
d3 <- FindNeighbors(d3, reduction = "pca", dims = 1:29)
d3 <- FindClusters(d3, resolution = 2, verbose = FALSE)
d3 <- RunTSNE(d3, reduction = "pca", dims = 1:20)

# Projecting singlet identities on TSNE visualization
DimPlot(d3, group.by = "HTO_maxID")
```

## load day 3 antibody data, unique to totalseq-A, already loaded if totalseq-B or -C.
```{r}
d3Adt <- Read10X(data.dir = "../citeseq/d3AdtCount/umi_count/", gene.column = 1)
d3Adt <- d3Adt[1:9,]
#d3Adt <- d3Adt[,d3Hto2[1,]<3000] # filter out large count cells
rownames(d3Adt) <- gsub('.{16}$', '', rownames(d3Adt))
rownames(d3Adt) <- paste0('Adt.', rownames(d3Adt))
joint.bcs <- intersect(colnames(d3), colnames(d3Adt))
d3Adt <- d3Adt[, joint.bcs]
d3 <- d3[, joint.bcs]
d3[["ADT"]] <- CreateAssayObject(counts = d3Adt)
d3 <- NormalizeData(d3, assay = "ADT", normalization.method = "CLR")
d3 <- ScaleData(d3, assay = "ADT")
RidgePlot(d3, features = c("Adt.CD11c", "Adt.CD11b", "Adt.B220",  "Adt.Gr1",   "Adt.MHCII", "Adt.SiglecH", "Adt.Sirpa", "Adt.CD24",  "Adt.F480"), ncol = 2)
```
